source: Oliver Byrne, "The First Six Books of the Elements of Euclid, in Which Coloured Diagrams and Symbols Are Used Instead of Letters for the Greater Ease of Learners", London 1847
ask: the second half of the seventh ruling on this mark (D483): "but also show me options for coloring faces of the shape also in the Byrne style"

areas.name: lune
areas.term: spherical triangle (two meridians + the equator arc between their feet)
areas.where: between the two meridians, on the visible face — the mark's own "area"

spherical.note: both foot angles are 90deg, which is what the two right-angle marks in the drawing state, so the excess is the pole angle alone

areas.name: north
areas.term: spherical lune (near equator semicircle + the limb's upper semicircle)
areas.where: everything above the near arc: the pole, both meridians, the right-angle marks

spherical.note: bounded by two great semicircles meeting where the equator crosses the limb, (62,78) and (178,78)

areas.name: south
areas.term: spherical lune (near equator semicircle + the limb's lower semicircle)
areas.where: between the near arc and the bottom of the silhouette

spherical.note: the north and south lunes tile the visible hemisphere exactly: their angles sum to 180deg

areas.name: disc
areas.term: the near hemisphere (what an orthographic view of a sphere shows)

spherical.note: a projection shows exactly one hemisphere, so colouring the near hemisphere means colouring the disc

shapeCountPrice.note: design/mark-geometry.mjs zips the painted report against the table and accepts exactly table+1 (the pole dot). A planted face makes 9 and both mark probes refuse: the refusal text is recorded per row in painted[].

rows.label: row C alone — the colouring the site ships today (nothing filled)
rows.byrne: the control: Byrne line colouring with no region. A face round without this row cannot say what a face costs.
rows.reading: the shipped mark: a colour names a line, and the figure has no area. Everything below is a delta from this measured line.

rows.label: the lune filled — the mark's own area, in the club red
rows.byrne: Byrne fills the region a proposition is about. Here that region is the spherical triangle between the two meridians and the near equator arc, and its area is fixed by the two right angles the mark already draws.
rows.reading: one area, one colour: "the red figure" is the strip of surface between the two lines, which is where the metaphor lives. The pair keep their two colours (row C), so the area names the BETWEEN, not a line.

rows.label: the south lune filled — the region below the near arc, in the club red
rows.byrne: the other reading of the same ink: colour the half the lines leave, so the equator becomes the boundary of a region rather than a line across a disc
rows.reading: the fill sits under the equator, so the sphere gains a near side and a far side: the dashed arc stays uncoloured and the solid arc reads as an edge of an area. The meridians run THROUGH the fill on their way up, so they are the lines the fill must not swallow.

rows.label: the north lune filled — the face the claim lives on, in the club blue
rows.byrne: Byrne colours the area a construction moves through; here the construction is the pair climbing to the pole, and the area they bound is everything above the equator
rows.reading: the biggest single region the drawing has (68.45% of the visible face) and the one that carries the pole, both meridians and the notation. It also puts the most line-ink over a fill, so it is where the two-bar squeeze bites hardest.

rows.label: two areas, two colours — lune red, south lune blue
rows.byrne: the literal Byrne sentence — "the squares of the blue and red lines" — where two regions are named by two colours so the prose can point at either without a letter
rows.reading: the two faces this drawing really does tile the figure with are the north and south lunes; this row takes the triangle inside the north face plus the south face, so the two fills are DISJOINT and meet only at the near arc. What it costs is a third name in a mark whose claim is about a pair of lines.

rows.label: the near hemisphere filled — the sphere as a body, in the palette's own grey
rows.byrne: Byrne's circles are regions as often as they are outlines; a filled limb is how 1847 printing says "this is a body, not a disc"
rows.reading: colouring the near hemisphere IS colouring the disc, so every one of the eight lines is drawn over the fill and the whole mark becomes lines-on-surface. This is the row that shows what the layer bar and the graphic bar cost at the same time.
